planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chesapeake, a U.S. National Arboretum hybrid (Viburnum utile x carlesii), bears glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and fragrant pink-budded white flowers, with good shade tolerance for a flowering viburnum.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Chesapeake tolerates more shade than most flowering viburnums while still blooming reliably. Bred at the U.S. National Arboretum from a cross of Viburnum utile and V. carlesii, Chesapeake combines the glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and refined habit of one parent with the intensely fragrant, pink-budded white flower clusters of the other, opening in mid-spring and perfuming the surrounding garden with a sweet, spicy scent. In milder winters it holds much of its foliage into the cold season, providing more structure and screening value than fully deciduous viburnums. It requires little routine care beyond an occasional shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood. A versatile shrub for a shaded foundation planting, woodland edge, or fragrance garden near a path or entry.

common_name: Red Bells Enkianthus (Deep Red-Veined Bell-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Red Bells bears bell-shaped flowers with deeper red veining than the straight species, followed by brilliant fall color.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, in the same conditions favored by rhododendrons and azaleas. Red Bells bears dangling clusters of small, cream-based, bell-shaped flowers etched with noticeably deeper red-pink veining than the species form, held along horizontally tiered branches in late spring, followed in fall by a spectacular display of red, orange, and yellow foliage color that ranks among the finest of any woodland shrub. Its tiered, layered branching habit provides distinctive year-round structure even without flowers or fall color. It combines beautifully with rhododendrons, azaleas, and other acid-loving woodland shrubs sharing the same partial-shade, moisture-retentive growing conditions. Prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Mount Airy Fothergilla (Premier Large Honey-Scented Fall-Color Fothergilla)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mount Airy is the premier large fothergilla selection, prized for reliable brilliant orange-red-yellow fall color and honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers, tolerating shadier sites than most flowering shrubs.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mount Airy tolerates shadier conditions than most spring-flowering shrubs while still delivering reliable bloom and fall color. Widely regarded as the finest fothergilla cultivar available, Mount Airy was discovered as a superior seedling at the Mount Airy Arboretum in Cincinnati and combines fragrant, honey-scented white bottlebrush flowers in mid-spring, before the leaves emerge, with an exceptionally consistent and vivid fall display blending brilliant orange, red, and yellow on the same plant, often on the same leaf, a color show that rivals or exceeds many more commonly planted shrubs. Its dense, rounded, well-behaved habit needs little pruning to look tidy. An outstanding, low-maintenance choice for the shaded or partly shaded shrub border, requiring no spraying and tolerating both heat and cold well within its range.

common_name: Aureomarginata Winter Daphne (Gold-Margined Fragrant Evergreen Daphne)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; Aureomarginata bears gold-margined variegated foliage and is noted as hardier and more garden-reliable than the plain green form of winter daphne, with intensely fragrant late-winter flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade, taking special care to avoid wet feet, since daphne is notoriously intolerant of poor drainage. Aureomarginata bears the same rounded, evergreen foliage as plain winter daphne but each leaf is neatly edged in gold, adding year-round color and interest beyond the famously fragrant bloom period, and nurserymen and gardeners widely consider it hardier and more reliable in cultivation than the plain green species form, which can be temperamental. Clusters of small, waxy, pink-flushed white flowers open in late winter to very early spring, releasing an intensely sweet fragrance that carries a remarkable distance for the size of the bloom, making it a prized shrub to site near an entry, path, or window. Avoid disturbing the roots once planted, and resist the urge to over-fertilize or overwater, since daphne performs best in lean, well-drained conditions with minimal interference.

common_name: Dwarf Himalayan Sweet Box (Low Spreading Deep-Shade Fragrant Groundcover Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade; this low, dense, spreading dwarf sweet box works as a groundcover for deep dry shade, bearing tiny, intensely fragrant winter flowers and black fruit.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, where it tolerates conditions few other evergreen shrubs will grow in, including dry shade once established. This dwarf, low-growing form of Himalayan sweet box spreads gradually by suckering rhizomes into a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen groundcover only knee-high or shorter, useful for massing beneath trees or along a shaded foundation where a taller shrub would be unwelcome. Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers hidden among the leaves in midwinter release a surprisingly powerful, sweet fragrance that carries well beyond the plant itself, followed by small black berries. It requires very little maintenance once established and tolerates deep shade, root competition, and periods of drought better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen. Water during extended dry spells the first year or two while roots establish.
